articleSummary: In Hanoi, a 4-year-old girl developed acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE) associated with Influenza A after fever and respiratory symptoms. She had continuous seizures and coma within 2 days; a throat swab tested positive for Influenza A. She received high-dose immunosuppressive therapy, renal replacement therapy, and intensive neurocritical care at National Children's Hospital, but brain injury progressed and she died two days after admission. ANE is a rare post-viral brain disease, often following Influenza A, caused by an excessive inflammatory response with cytokine release that disrupts the blood-brain barrier, leading to edema, necrosis, coagulopathy and multi-organ involvement. It typically affects children 2-5 years old. No unified treatment protocol exists; early immunosuppression within 24 hours of neurological symptoms may help some cases. Influenza in children is usually mild but can cause pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalitis, respiratory failure or multi-organ injury. Parents should seek urgent care for high fever with seizures or breathing problems; vaccination is advised.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus, a rare filovirus relative of Ebola, is fueling outbreak in the DRC with spillover into Uganda. Bundibugyo causes severe hemorrhagic fever with vascular leakage, multi-organ failure; transmission occurs via direct contact with infected fluids, endangering families and health workers, especially in under-resourced hospitals. Symptoms overlap malaria/typhoid, necessitating laboratory confirmation. No licensed Bundibugyo-specific vaccine or therapy exists; although vaccines against other filoviruses show promise, dedicated tools are lacking. articleSummary: Dengue fever is spreading in many places even when rainfall is absent. articleHeadline: Buruli Ulcer: The Silent Flesheater Hiding in Our Waters
articleSummary: Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans in rural Ghanaian river basins, is a neglected tropical skin infection. It begins as a painless skin nodule near slow-moving rivers, swamps or wetlands; the toxin mycolactone damages tissue and suppresses local immunity, so initial lesions are painless with no fever. If untreated, progression leads to a large ulcer with deep tissue damage, potential scarring and disability. Transmission is not fully understood; environmental reservoirs exist with exposure through farming, fishing, or wading; minor skin breaks in muddy water may introduce bacteria. Children under 15 are disproportionately affected. Early treatment is highly effective with antibiotics (rifampicin plus clarithromycin or streptomycin) for several weeks, along with wound care and physiotherapy. Delays and reliance on traditional remedies worsen outcomes. Public health messages should promote prompt clinic visits for persistent painless skin lesions to prevent disability.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus, an Ebola-like filovirus, triggers a significant Central Africa outbreak with 695 confirmed cases and 138 deaths in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda as of mid-June 2026. Previously recorded outbreaks occurred in Uganda (2007) and DRC (2012); the current wave surpasses prior events in scale and geographic spread. Transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids, risking family members, caregivers, and health workers, particularly in settings with weak infection-control practices. Early symptoms resemble malaria and typhoid, but progression leads to severe hemorrhagic fever, endothelial damage, uncontrolled bleeding, and multi-organ failure. Diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation; access to specialized labs is limited, with samples traveling long distances and delays hampering isolation and contact tracing. articleSummary: Rajarshi Mandal, a 16-year-old Lexington High School student from Lexington, Massachusetts, built an ordinary differential equation malaria transmission model to optimize the allocation of insecticide-treated bed nets under limited supply. Using a framework that simulates transmission with seasonality, insecticide resistance, net degradation, and remote-area logistics, his results show the same global net supply could prevent twice as many infections if nets are distributed where they have the greatest impact, rather than by population alone. The study addresses backward bifurcation to ensure transmission persistence under realistic conditions and derives a reproduction number reflecting transmission risk. Mandal abandoned an initial Deep Q Network after instability and now directly scores allocations. The work highlights global nets distributed around 200 million annually and earned him a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship, with an image from the Democratic Republic of Congo illustrating logistical hurdles that can impede even well-planned programs.

articleHeadline: Kasus Influenza A Merebak, Pakar UGM Bagikan 6 Langkah Cegah Penularan
articleSummary: Influenza A cases are rising in Indonesia, with Ministry of Health data up to 12 September 2026 showing a 38% positivity rate for lab-confirmed influenza in week 35, up from 22% the prior week. Of 175 specimens tested, 66 were positive, with the majority identified as influenza A(H1N1)pdm09. The Jakarta report notes the circulating A(H1N1) lineage is a genetic descendant of the 2009 pandemic virus that has undergone mutations. In response, Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM) microbiology experts advocate six steps to prevent transmission, while cautioning against overreaction. Prof. Tri Wibawa emphasizes that despite genetic changes, mitigation remains important to reduce spread. The article highlights the need for ongoing laboratory confirmation and public health measures to curb transmission as influenza A(H1N1) continues to circulate in Indonesia.

articleSummary: As of 21 September 2026, dengue fever in Tamil Nadu shows rapid spread with 228 new cases in a single day, including 79 in Chennai. The state’s total dengue cases reach 17,277, averaging about 200 daily. In response, government hospitals have opened dedicated dengue wards and authorities continue surveillance, though the outbreak persists and criticisms about containment remain. Health experts stress vector control to curb transmission, noting that dengue-carrying mosquitoes breed in clean, standing water; identifying and eliminating standing-water sites is essential. Officials urge swift actions to reduce breeding and prevent further spread across Tamil Nadu.

articleSummary: On 20 September 2026, Tamil Nadu reported 228 dengue fever cases in a single day, with Chennai accounting for 79 dengue cases and 29 chikungunya cases in the same city. Madurai district recorded 38 dengue cases over the previous 21 days. Statewide totals rise to 17,277 dengue and 4,648 chikungunya cases to date. The districts with the highest burden include Chennai, Coimbatore, Erode, Tiruppur, Salem, and Krishnagiri. Authorities have intensified vector-control measures and set up medical camps in affected areas to curb transmission. The outbreak is concentrated in urban and peri-urban regions, prompting ongoing public health interventions to suppress mosquito populations and prevent further spread.
